title: Does temporal discounting explain unhealthy behavior? A systematic review and reinforcement learning perspective

subsections.section_title: Conceptual Background and Framing of Temporal Discounting in Health Behavior
subsections.subsection_title: Foundational Theories of Intertemporal Choice and Temporal Discounting
subsections.content:
Foundational theories of intertemporal choice were shaped by the tension between normative consistency and observed impulsiveness. Classical economics largely treated time preference as a stable depreciation of future utility, but early critiques already emphasized myopia and dynamic inconsistency. Strotz’s analysis formalized the idea that non-exponential discounting can generate plans that are optimal ex ante yet abandoned ex post, thereby motivating precommitment ref [5]. This insight helped redefine impulsive choice as a problem of changing preferences over time rather than simple ignorance or irrationality.

The decisive behavioral turn came from Ainslie’s proposal that delayed rewards are discounted hyperbolically, producing preference reversals as smaller-sooner rewards become imminent ref [1]. This framework connected impulsiveness, self-control, and commitment devices within a unified account, and later experimental work showed such reversals directly in human delayed-reward choices ref [2]. Hyperbolic and quasi-hyperbolic formulations subsequently became central because they capture present bias while remaining analytically tractable, as illustrated in economic models of self-control and illiquid commitment technologies ref [3].

At the same time, foundational theory also broadened beyond simple impatience. Critical reviews distinguished pure time preference from other determinants of intertemporal choice, including uncertainty, consumption complementarity, and changing tastes ref [6]. Loewenstein further argued that anticipation itself can carry utility or disutility, so delayed outcomes may be savored or dreaded rather than merely discounted ref [7]. This opened the door to cases of negative time preference, in which individuals prefer postponement of pleasurable outcomes or hastening of aversive ones ref [8]. Together, these theories established temporal discounting as a richer family of mechanisms than constant exponential impatience alone ref [5], ref [6].

subsections.section_title: Conceptual Background and Framing of Temporal Discounting in Health Behavior
subsections.subsection_title: From General Discounting to Health-Specific Time Preferences
subsections.content:
A central move in health economics was to distinguish generic impatience from preferences over health trajectories. Grossman’s health capital model already implied that health is a durable stock yielding healthy time, so intertemporal health choices cannot be reduced to ordinary consumption timing alone ref [8]. Subsequent work therefore asked whether discounting for health should equal discounting for money in cost-effectiveness analysis, or whether health-specific time preference warrants separate treatment ref [11]. This shift was conceptually important because health outcomes differ from money in reversibility, uncertainty, embodiment, and their links to morbidity and mortality.

Empirically, time preference for health is not a simple translation of monetary discounting. Studies comparing domains show that individuals often use different rates for health and money, with relatively weak cross-domain consistency ref [11], and that the comparison depends on whether choices are framed as private or social trade-offs ref [10], or whether health is explicitly tradable against money ref [12]. Population-based evidence further suggests marked heterogeneity across health scenarios, including occasional zero or negative time preference for some future health outcomes ref [13]. Meta-regression evidence also indicates that estimated health discount rates vary systematically with delay and gain-loss framing, helping explain the wide dispersion in published estimates ref [9].

These findings support the idea of health-specific time preferences rather than a single, domain-general discount parameter. Methodologically, they also motivate models that go beyond constant exponential discounting. Axiomatic tests in the health domain reject strict stationarity and favor decreasing timing aversion for at least some outcomes ref [15], while broader debates in cost-effectiveness analysis stress that the choice of discounting framework has direct consequences for valuing prevention and other interventions with delayed benefits ref [11]. Taken together, the literature reframes temporal discounting in health behavior as a domain-sensitive construct shaped by the meaning of health states, the social perspective adopted, and the structure of intertemporal trade-offs ref [10], ref [11].

subsections.section_title: Conceptual Background and Framing of Temporal Discounting in Health Behavior
subsections.subsection_title: Neural and Reward-System Perspectives on Delay and Anticipation
subsections.content:
Neural accounts of temporal discounting emphasize an interaction between valuation circuits sensitive to immediacy and control-related circuits that support prospective comparison. In a highly influential fMRI study, choices involving an immediately available monetary reward preferentially recruited ventral striatum, medial orbitofrontal cortex, and medial prefrontal regions, whereas lateral prefrontal and posterior parietal areas were engaged more uniformly across intertemporal choices ref [17]. Importantly, the relative balance of these systems predicted whether participants selected the smaller-sooner or larger-later option, linking neural competition directly to observed impatience ref [17].

Subsequent work showed that this pattern is not restricted to abstract monetary outcomes. Using thirsty participants choosing between immediate and delayed juice or water rewards over minutes, limbic reward-related regions again responded more strongly when an immediate option was present, while dorsolateral prefrontal and parietal areas tracked intertemporal choice more generally ref [16]. This extension to primary rewards is important for health behavior, because many unhealthy acts involve biologically salient rewards—food, alcohol, nicotine, or immediate symptom relief—whose neural coding may be especially sensitive to short delays and visceral state ref [16].

A complementary literature shows that anticipation itself can carry positive or negative utility. Neuroimaging of waiting for aversive electric shocks found that people who behaviorally preferred to expedite pain exhibited earlier and more sustained activity in posterior insula, somatosensory cortex, and caudal anterior cingulate during the waiting period, consistent with a neural signature of dread ref [18]. Together with evidence that anticipatory utility can shape intertemporal value beyond simple discounting, these findings suggest that health decisions are influenced not only by devaluation of delayed outcomes but also by the affective burden or attraction of waiting itself. From a reinforcement-learning perspective, this implies that choice reflects temporally extended prediction, anticipatory states, and state-dependent reward signals, rather than a single stationary discount parameter ref [16], ref [17], ref [18].

subsections.section_title: Conceptual Background and Framing of Temporal Discounting in Health Behavior
subsections.subsection_title: Temporal Discounting in Health Behavior and Prevention
subsections.content:
Temporal discounting is especially relevant to prevention because many health-protective actions impose immediate costs—effort, inconvenience, discomfort, or foregone pleasure—while their benefits are delayed and probabilistic. In this framing, lower discounting should promote behaviors such as vaccination, screening, medication adherence, and lifestyle change. Early work explicitly linked “value for the future” to preventive health behavior, but also warned that the mapping from elicited time preferences to real-world action may be weaker than theory suggests ref [4], ref [5].

Evidence on preventive behaviors is mixed. In an influential vaccination study, more future-oriented monetary time preferences were associated with influenza vaccine uptake, but the effect was small and did not generalize to health-specific or sequence-based measures ref [5]. Chapman et al. later extended this logic to influenza vaccination, antihypertensive adherence, and cholesterol-lowering medication, again finding weak or inconsistent associations between hypothetical discounting measures and actual preventive behavior ref [4]. Earlier population evidence likewise found only modest links between discounting and behaviors such as smoking, exercise, seat-belt use, and dental examinations ref [6].

These findings suggest that temporal discounting is best viewed as one determinant among many, rather than a unitary explanation for unhealthy behavior. Beliefs about treatment effectiveness, perceived side effects, habits, self-control demands, and environmental constraints often explain more variance than discounting alone ref [4], ref [5], ref [7]. This helps distinguish preventive health behaviors from some addictive behaviors, where discounting gradients are often larger and more reliable ref [8], ref [9]. For prevention research, the key implication is not to abandon intertemporal models, but to embed them in broader accounts of valuation, learning, and context-sensitive choice ref [10].

subsections.section_title: Conceptual Background and Framing of Temporal Discounting in Health Behavior
subsections.subsection_title: Methodological and Modeling Considerations
subsections.content:
Methodological variation is a central reason why evidence linking temporal discounting to unhealthy behavior remains heterogeneous. Studies differ in reward domain (money, food, health states), time horizon, gain-versus-loss framing, outcome magnitude, and whether discounting is inferred from hypothetical choices, experiential tasks, or stated health preferences. These design choices matter because discount rates are often not stable traits across domains, and verbal descriptions alone can obscure the assumptions built into a task or model ref [2], ref [3], ref [4].

A related issue is model specification. Exponential, hyperbolic, quasi-hyperbolic, and attribute-based models can fit the same data with different psychological interpretations, while good fit alone does not guarantee theoretical adequacy ref [5], ref [6], ref [7]. Computational modeling is therefore valuable not merely for prediction but for clarifying mechanisms, forcing explicit assumptions, and improving reproducibility across laboratories ref [2]. In health applications, richer models can separate impatience from correlated processes such as risk sensitivity, reward valuation, learning, and self-control costs, which are otherwise easily conflated in simple choice summaries ref [8], ref [9].

From a reinforcement-learning perspective, unhealthy behavior may reflect not only steep discounting but also biased state representations, maladaptive temporal-credit assignment, cue-triggered policy selection, or distorted estimates of delayed health consequences ref [10], ref [11]. This argues for combining discounting tasks with sequential paradigms, longitudinal designs, and hierarchical estimation, and for reporting model comparison, parameter recovery, and out-of-sample prediction rather than relying exclusively on single-parameter discount rates ref [2], ref [7], ref [11].

subsections.section_title: Systematic Review Methodology and Empirical Evidence Across Health Domains
subsections.subsection_title: Methodological Foundations and Theoretical Reviews
subsections.content:
Methodological and theoretical reviews have framed delay discounting as a central operationalization of intertemporal choice in health behavior, while also emphasizing substantial heterogeneity in tasks, commodities, and model specification. Core reviews distinguish adjusting-amount, adjusting-delay, and brief questionnaire approaches, and note that estimates may be summarized either parametrically (e.g., hyperbolic k) or nonparametrically (e.g., area under the curve), with implications for comparability across studies ref [23]. This measurement pluralism is useful, but it complicates synthesis when studies mix hypothetical and experiential tasks, monetary and health outcomes, or different delay horizons ref [23].

A second foundational theme is whether discounting should be treated as a stable trait, a state-sensitive process, or both. Reviews of human and addiction research converge on the view that discounting shows moderate test-retest stability yet remains malleable under deprivation, framing, cognitive load, and treatment-related manipulations ref [22], ref [23]. This perspective is important methodologically because many associations between steep discounting and unhealthy behavior are cross-sectional; accordingly, causal interpretation requires longitudinal or experimental designs that can separate antecedent risk from consequences of use or illness ref [22], ref [23], ref [4].

Theoretical reviews further broaden the construct beyond a unitary notion of impulsivity. De Wit argues that delay discounting, behavioral inhibition, and attentional lapses reflect partially dissociable processes, cautioning against treating all impulsive behavior as equivalent ref [4]. Complementing this, the competing neurobehavioral decision systems account interprets steep discounting as an imbalance between valuation systems favoring immediacy and executive control systems supporting delayed outcomes, and uses intervention studies to motivate mechanistic hypotheses about cognitive training, neuromodulation, and reframing ref [22]. Together, these reviews provide the methodological basis for the empirical literature across smoking, alcohol, obesity, and preventive health behavior, while also motivating reinforcement-learning perspectives that distinguish immediate reward valuation, state dependence, and control costs from a single discount-rate explanation ref [22], ref [4].

subsections.section_title: Systematic Review Methodology and Empirical Evidence Across Health Domains
subsections.subsection_title: Smoking, Nicotine Dependence, and Cessation
subsections.content:
Smoking is among the most replicated health domains in temporal-discounting research. Cross-sectional laboratory studies consistently show steeper discounting among current smokers than never smokers, with evidence that this difference generalizes across monetary outcomes and, to a lesser extent, health outcomes [1]. Discounting is also associated more strongly with nicotine dependence severity than with simple smoking quantity: steeper discounting correlates with FTND scores, but not reliably with cigarettes per day, suggesting that temporal myopia may track dependence processes rather than sheer consumption volume ref [13].

Developmental evidence indicates that these associations emerge early. Adolescents experimenting with cigarettes exhibit discounting rates intermediate between never smokers and daily smokers, and in several analyses resemble regular smokers more than nonsmokers, supporting the view that elevated discounting may precede entrenched tobacco use rather than merely result from it ref [10]. Complementing this, adolescent work suggests a psychosocial pathway whereby perceived stress is associated with smoking status partly through elevated delay discounting ref [16]. At the population level, panel-survey analyses likewise link higher discount rates to smoking participation, with additional roles for present bias and related time-inconsistency measures ref [28].

Temporal discounting is also prognostic for cessation outcomes. Among highly dependent, lower-SES smokers, steeper discounting independently predicts poorer response to tobacco-dependence treatment even after accounting for locus of control, impulsiveness, stress, and dependence severity ref [12]. In pregnancy-related contexts, higher baseline discounting predicts postpartum relapse among women who had quit during pregnancy ref [14]. Longitudinal household data further indicate that smokers with longer-term time preferences are more likely to achieve cessation over time ref [15]. Overall, smoking studies provide some of the strongest evidence that temporal discounting is not merely correlated with unhealthy behavior, but is meaningfully implicated in initiation, dependence, relapse, and treatment response.

subsections.section_title: Systematic Review Methodology and Empirical Evidence Across Health Domains
subsections.subsection_title: Alcohol and Other Substance Use Disorders
subsections.content:
Evidence from alcohol and other substance use disorders generally supports an association between steeper delay discounting and more severe addictive behavior, but with important heterogeneity across substances and outcomes. In alcohol research, both social and problem drinkers exhibit hyperbolic discounting, with steeper discounting among heavier or more problematic drinkers ref [38]. More recent behavioral-economic work further suggests that discounting is linked more closely to alcohol use disorder (AUD) symptoms than to simple consumption volume, and covaries with alcohol demand and craving ref [35]. In adolescents, heavy drinking is likewise associated with greater discounting of delayed monetary and alcohol rewards, alongside alcohol-cue attentional bias, indicating that impulsive intertemporal choice and cue-reactivity may co-occur early in the course of risky use ref [10].

Cross-substance comparisons indicate that the discounting signal is not uniform. Heroin- and cocaine-dependent individuals discount delayed rewards more steeply than controls, and more steeply than alcohol-dependent participants in one direct comparison, suggesting substance-specific gradients in valuation of the future ref [33]. Cocaine dependence is also associated with rapid discounting in laboratory studies ref [20], and steeper discounting predicts poorer treatment response among cocaine-dependent outpatients ref [18]. Among adolescents in treatment more broadly, higher discounting predicts worse substance abuse treatment outcomes, reinforcing its clinical prognostic value beyond cross-sectional case-control contrasts ref [17].

Findings for cannabis are comparatively mixed. Current marijuana dependence shows only a trend toward elevated monetary discounting relative to former users and controls, although marijuana itself is discounted more steeply than money within dependent users ref [12]. This weaker and less consistent pattern than for opioids or stimulants is important for theory: temporal discounting appears to mark a transdiagnostic vulnerability process, but one whose magnitude depends on drug class, reward commodity, and clinical endpoint. From a reinforcement-learning perspective, such variation is compatible with discounting acting not as a single cause of unhealthy behavior, but as one component of a broader choice architecture that also includes cue-driven value inflation, craving, and treatment-contingent reinforcement ref [35].

subsections.section_title: Systematic Review Methodology and Empirical Evidence Across Health Domains
subsections.subsection_title: Preventive Health Behavior and General Health Outcomes
subsections.content:
Evidence linking temporal discounting to preventive health behavior is mixed and generally weaker than in addiction domains. Early survey work on influenza vaccination found only a small association between future-oriented monetary time preferences and uptake of a free workplace flu shot, while parallel health-domain discounting measures were not predictive and beliefs about vaccine effectiveness were more important correlates ref [20]. This pattern was reinforced by a broader review of preventive behaviors, where scenario-based discounting showed weak or null associations with influenza vaccination, antihypertensive adherence, and cholesterol-lowering medication adherence ref [6].

At the same time, population-based studies using larger samples and econometric imputation of individual discount rates suggest that steep discounting can matter for routine health maintenance. Using Health and Retirement Study data, Bradford reported that respondents in the highest discount-rate group were less likely to obtain mammograms, Pap smears, prostate exams, cholesterol testing, dental visits, and flu shots, and were also less likely to exercise and remain nonsmokers ref [19]. Related work on cancer prevention similarly argues that screening and control behaviors are prototypical intertemporal choices, because they impose immediate inconvenience or discomfort for uncertain long-run benefit ref [5].

Taken together, this literature supports a nuanced conclusion: temporal discounting is better viewed as one contributor to preventive health behavior than as a dominant explanation of general health outcomes. Future orientation or “value for the future” appears conceptually relevant, but empirical effect sizes are often modest and sensitive to measurement domain, task framing, and competing determinants such as beliefs, access, and prior habits ref [6]. This interpretation is also consistent with broader theoretical accounts that frame prevention as an investment in health capital, where discounting interacts with risk perceptions, resources, and the structure of delayed health returns ref [20], ref [19].

subsections.section_title: Systematic Review Methodology and Empirical Evidence Across Health Domains
subsections.subsection_title: Obesity, Food Reward, and Other Clinical Health Domains
subsections.content:
Evidence linking temporal discounting to obesity is suggestive but more heterogeneous than in addiction research. Cross-sectional studies indicate that steeper discounting is associated with higher weight status, particularly in women, and may extend to adolescent populations with overlapping risk behaviors such as smoking [ref 1], [ref 3]. Importantly, obesity-related findings increasingly support an interactional account in which discounting is not merely a trait marker of impulsivity, but one component of a broader reward-control imbalance involving food cue responsiveness and inhibitory control [ref 1].

A key laboratory study in overweight and obese women showed that food reward sensitivity predicted greater intake of palatable foods in the absence of hunger only among individuals with steeper delay discounting; when discounting was lower, food reward sensitivity was not associated with overeating [ref 1]. This pattern aligns with reinforcement-learning perspectives in which unhealthy eating reflects a dominance of immediate reward valuation over prospective outcome integration. Convergent developmental evidence comes from a longitudinal cohort showing that failure to delay gratification at age 4 predicted higher risk of overweight at age 11, although this association was attenuated after accounting for maternal weight status, suggesting partial familial or environmental confounding [ref 2].

Related work in adolescent smokers found that obese smokers discounted delayed monetary rewards more steeply than healthy-weight smokers, consistent with potentially additive risk across obesity and nicotine use [ref 3]. Beyond weight status per se, discounting has also been linked to food-specific reinforcement and body fat, implying that valuation processes may generalize across monetary and primary rewards [ref 4], [ref 5], [ref 6]. Still, this literature remains constrained by reliance on hypothetical rewards, cross-sectional designs, and inconsistent sex and age effects. Other clinical domains such as eating pathology and comorbid self-regulation disorders likely require models that integrate discounting with cue-reactivity, habit learning, and state-dependent control failure rather than treating discounting as a standalone explanation [ref 7], [ref 8].

subsections.section_title: Theoretical Evaluation of Hyperbolic Discounting and Preference Reversal
subsections.subsection_title: Foundations of Hyperbolic Discounting and Impulsiveness
subsections.content:
Hyperbolic discounting emerged as a corrective to exponential models that cannot easily accommodate impulsiveness despite stable information sets. Ainslie’s behavioral account argued that the subjective value of delayed rewards declines in a strongly concave, approximately hyperbolic manner, so that a smaller-sooner option can temporarily dominate a larger-later one as the moment of consumption approaches, making impulsive choice an endogenous feature of valuation rather than mere error or ignorance ref [1]. This insight extends Strotz’s original critique of dynamically inconsistent intertemporal choice and provides the psychological foundation for later economic models of self-control problems.

The central implication is that impulsiveness reflects present-biased weighting, not simply globally high impatience. Under hyperbolic discounting, relative preferences are time-sensitive: long-run plans may favor abstention, saving, or prevention, while short-run choice shifts toward immediately gratifying options ref [1]. This formulation helps explain why unhealthy behaviors often coexist with explicit intentions to avoid them, and why agents seek self-binding arrangements. Laibson formalized this logic in a quasi-hyperbolic framework, showing that present bias generates demand for commitment technologies and predicts behavior that resembles self-imposed liquidity constraints and other practical devices for limiting future temptation ref [3].

From a reinforcement-learning perspective, hyperbolic discounting is especially relevant because it links impulsiveness to the temporal credit-assignment problem. A steep near-term decline in value amplifies the salience of proximal rewards relative to delayed health benefits, making myopic policies locally attractive even when they are globally suboptimal. In this sense, impulsiveness can be interpreted as a structurally induced policy bias under non-exponential valuation rather than a simple failure of rational calculation ref [1], ref [3]. This conceptualization provides a useful bridge from descriptive choice theory to computational accounts of unhealthy behavior.

subsections.section_title: Theoretical Evaluation of Hyperbolic Discounting and Preference Reversal
subsections.subsection_title: Preference Reversal and Temporal Choice Dynamics
subsections.content:
Preference reversal is the central dynamic implication that distinguishes hyperbolic from exponential discounting. Under decreasing impatience, an option preferred when both outcomes are remote can lose to a smaller-sooner option as both rewards approach the present, violating stationarity and generating time-inconsistent plans. Classic experimental evidence with real rewards documented such reversals for most participants, supporting the claim that discount rates rise sharply near the present rather than remaining constant over time ref [2], ref [3], ref [4].

At the same time, later work complicates a simple present-bias interpretation. Kable and Glimcher show that individuals often overweight the soonest available option even when neither option is immediate, producing an “as soon as possible” effect that attenuates or eliminates the impulsive reversals predicted by standard quasi-hyperbolic models ref [46]. Related behavioral work similarly suggests that discounting may depend on intervals, reference delays, or subadditivity rather than on immediacy alone ref [5], ref [6], ref [7]. These findings imply that temporal choice dynamics may reflect contextual comparison processes as much as a fixed parameter of impatience.

For unhealthy behavior, this distinction is consequential. If reversals arise mainly from present bias, interventions should target commitment and immediate temptation; if they instead reflect shifting temporal reference points, then reframing near-term and long-term health outcomes may be equally important. Neuroeconomic evidence also weakens a strict dual-system account by showing value signals for both immediate and delayed rewards rather than a system specialized only for immediacy ref [46], ref [8], ref [9]. A reinforcement-learning perspective is useful here: preference reversals can be interpreted as state- and horizon-dependent changes in subjective value computation, rather than as stable trait impulsivity alone ref [10].

subsections.section_title: Theoretical Evaluation of Hyperbolic Discounting and Preference Reversal
subsections.subsection_title: State Dependence and Applied Contexts of Time Inconsistency
subsections.content:
Time inconsistency in unhealthy behavior is often amplified by state dependence: preferences are shaped not only by delay, but also by transient physiological and affective states. In food choice, hunger shifts both immediate and advance preferences, and individuals imperfectly forecast how future appetite will alter valuation. Read and van Leeuwen’s field experiment shows that current hunger contaminates advance snack choices and that choices become more unhealthy when consumption is immediate, indicating a joint role for visceral-state prediction errors and present bias rather than discounting alone ref [47]. This pattern aligns with the broader visceral-factor account, in which ‘hot’ states narrow attention toward immediate relief and reduce the influence of long-run goals.

Applied contexts make this interaction especially salient. In addiction, cue-induced craving can reactivate drug-seeking long after withdrawal has ended, implying that temporal choice is conditioned by internal and environmental states rather than governed by a stable discount parameter ref [48]. Reviews of cue reactivity and relapse similarly show that craving, stress, and drug-associated stimuli can increase impulsive responding and undermine abstinence plans, even when individuals endorse long-term health goals (Field et al., 2004; Carter and Tiffany, 1999; Sinha, 2001). Empirically, craving is associated with alcohol demand and steeper discounting in alcohol use disorders, suggesting that valuation becomes state-contingent within episodes of temptation.

From a reinforcement-learning perspective, these findings are consistent with dynamic policies whose value estimates depend on latent motivational state and cue context. Apparent preference reversals may therefore reflect shifts in state representation or incentive salience, not merely a fixed hyperbolic discount function. This helps explain why interventions that change context, precommitment opportunities, or exposure to tempting cues can alter behavior without necessarily changing underlying long-run preferences ref [47], ref [48].

subsections.section_title: Reinforcement Learning Accounts of Cue-Driven and Habitual Unhealthy Behavior
subsections.subsection_title: Model-Based and Model-Free Reinforcement Learning in Habitual Choice
subsections.content:
A central reinforcement-learning account of habitual choice distinguishes model-based control, which evaluates actions by consulting an internal model of action–outcome contingencies, from model-free control, which relies on cached values shaped by past reinforcement [3]. This distinction provides a mechanistic reinterpretation of the classic goal-directed versus habitual dichotomy: model-based choice is flexible and outcome-sensitive, whereas model-free choice is computationally cheap but relatively insensitive to changes in outcome value or contingency [3]. In unhealthy behavior, this framework is attractive because repeated consumption of calorie-dense food, nicotine, or alcohol may progressively shift behavior from deliberative evaluation toward cue-triggered responding.

Empirical work supports partially dissociable neural substrates for these controllers. In rodents, ventral striatum and orbitofrontal cortex are both necessary when learning depends on changes in reward identity, a hallmark of model-based inference, whereas orbitofrontal cortex is not required for purely value-based unblocking that can be supported by model-free mechanisms [1]. More broadly, reviews of action control converge on corticostriatal specialization, with dorsomedial/prefrontal circuits linked to goal-directed control and dorsolateral striatal circuits linked to habit expression [3]. Human neuroimaging similarly shows that posterior dorsolateral striatum tracks extensively trained, habit-like responding, whereas ventromedial/orbitofrontal regions support outcome-based valuation and caudate-related signals are engaged during model-based planning and contingency-sensitive choice [3].

This architecture is especially relevant for unhealthy behavior because it implies that maladaptive choice need not reflect only steep temporal discounting; it may also arise when cue-rich environments favor model-free control or weaken model-based oversight. Consistent with this view, pharmacological enhancement of dopamine with L-DOPA increases the weighting of model-based over model-free control in a two-step decision task [2], suggesting that neuromodulatory state can shift the balance between prospective evaluation and habit. Thus, reinforcement-learning accounts complement intertemporal-choice explanations by showing how repeated exposure, environmental regularities, and state-dependent arbitration between controllers can produce persistent unhealthy behavior even when long-run consequences are understood [2,3].

subsections.section_title: Reinforcement Learning Accounts of Cue-Driven and Habitual Unhealthy Behavior
subsections.subsection_title: Habit Formation and Repetition in Everyday Unhealthy Behavior
subsections.content:
Habit accounts are particularly useful for everyday unhealthy behavior because many such actions are repeated in stable contexts and become increasingly cue driven rather than explicitly deliberated. Neal, Wood, and Quinn define habits as automatic response dispositions elicited by recurring situational cues, and diary evidence suggests that a large share of everyday action is repeated in the same locations and routines, including behaviors such as fast-food eating and exercise ref [52]. In this view, unhealthy consumption often persists not because people continuously re-evaluate its benefits, but because contexts such as time of day, place, or social company retrieve cached response tendencies ref [52].

Ouellette and Wood’s meta-analytic account sharpens this point by distinguishing two routes from past behavior to future behavior: direct repetition under high-opportunity, stable conditions, and intention-mediated action when contexts are unstable or the behavior is infrequent ref [53]. For everyday health behaviors, this implies that repeated snacking, sedentary leisure, or routine fast-food purchase may be better predicted by past enactment than by current stated goals once habits are strong ref [53]. This framework aligns naturally with reinforcement-learning distinctions: repeated reward in a stable environment can shift control toward cached action values and away from prospective evaluation, even when explicit intentions change.

An important implication is that changing unhealthy habits requires disrupting cue-behavior contingencies, not merely changing beliefs. Neal et al. note that informational interventions often fail when behavior is already habitual, whereas context change can restore intentional control ref [52]. Likewise, Ouellette and Wood argue that stable repetition is the critical substrate of habit, so intervention windows may arise when routines are naturally perturbed ref [53]. From an RL perspective, this corresponds to weakening established stimulus-action values and creating conditions for new policies to be learned, helping explain why everyday unhealthy behavior is often persistent, context specific, and only partially related to temporal discounting per se.

subsections.section_title: Reinforcement Learning Accounts of Cue-Driven and Habitual Unhealthy Behavior
subsections.subsection_title: Addiction, Delay Discounting, and Intertemporal Choice
subsections.content:
Addiction has long been framed as an intertemporal choice problem: the agent repeatedly trades immediate pharmacological reward against delayed health, social, and financial costs. In economics, rational addiction models explain persistent use through forward-looking optimization with consumption capital, adjacent complementarity, and sensitivity to permanent price changes, thus showing that apparently compulsive behavior need not be wholly myopic ref [54]. By contrast, behavioral accounts of hyperbolic discounting emphasize preference reversals and self-control failures, whereby near-term drug reward is overweighted relative to delayed harms, making relapse and underinvestment in abstinence more likely ref [3].

Empirically, steeper delay discounting is one of the most robust correlates of substance-use disorders and related relapse risk, supporting the view that excessive discounting is a trans-disease vulnerability rather than a drug-specific anomaly ref [22]. Neuroeconomic evidence further suggests that intertemporal choice recruits partially dissociable valuation systems: limbic and paralimbic regions respond preferentially when immediate rewards are available, whereas lateral prefrontal and parietal regions are engaged more generally during deliberation over delayed options ref [5]. This dual-systems pattern aligns naturally with addiction theories in which cue-triggered immediacy competes with executive control.

From a reinforcement-learning perspective, these findings imply that addiction is not explained by temporal discounting alone. Rather, discounting interacts with learned cue values, state-dependent craving, and policy control: drugs and drug cues can amplify the subjective value of immediate outcomes, while impaired prospective evaluation weakens sensitivity to delayed consequences. Reviews grounded in the competing neurobehavioral decision systems account therefore treat discounting as a mutable decision process, potentially altered by working-memory training, framing, or contingency management ref [22]. This makes intertemporal choice a useful bridge between classic addiction economics, computational accounts of valuation, and RL models of maladaptive habit persistence.

subsections.section_title: Reinforcement Learning Accounts of Cue-Driven and Habitual Unhealthy Behavior
subsections.subsection_title: Temporal-Difference Learning and Discounting Extensions
subsections.content:
Temporal-difference (TD) learning provides the canonical computational account of how cue values are acquired through prediction errors, but its standard formulation assumes exponential discounting of future outcomes [1]. This assumption is problematic for unhealthy behavior, because many relevant choices—smoking, overeating, or drug taking versus delayed health benefits—show dynamically inconsistent, often hyperbolic, valuation. A key extension therefore asks whether TD-like learning can reproduce present-biased preferences without abandoning recursive value updating [2].

One route is to derive hyperbolic-looking choice from a population of exponential learners. Kurth-Nelson and Redish show that a distribution of micro-agents, each with its own exponential discount factor and value estimate, can collectively generate approximately hyperbolic discounting while preserving TD-style prediction errors [1]. Importantly, they also show that discounting across chained states requires distributed value representations, not merely a direct substitution of a hyperbolic function into a one-step TD update, otherwise multi-step sequences collapse back toward exponential behavior [1]. This point is especially relevant for unhealthy habits, where long action chains separate cues, consumption, and delayed health costs.

A complementary strategy is to formulate hyperbolic discounting recursively. Alexander and Brown introduce hyperbolically discounted TD learning (HDTD), in which the effective hazard or discount term depends on current state value, yielding an exact recursive counterpart to standard hyperbolic discounting [2]. Their model captures preference reversals and can accommodate reward-magnitude effects by scaling discounting with expected reward per trial [2]. HDTD also outperforms average-reward TD in accounting for sensitivity to the temporal pattern of reward delivery, suggesting that risk-sensitive discounting, rather than only reward-rate maximization, may better explain some maladaptive choice patterns [2].

Taken together, these extensions broaden the reinforcement-learning perspective on temporal discounting. Rather than treating steep discounting as a static preference parameter, they model it as emerging from the architecture of prediction, representation, and state transition learning itself [1,2]. For unhealthy behavior, this implies that impulsive consumption may reflect not only a taste for immediacy, but also how agents decompose time, represent future states, and propagate delayed consequences through learned value functions.

subsections.section_title: Future Research Directions and Translational Implications
subsections.subsection_title: Developmental, Genetic, and Endophenotypic Pathways
subsections.content:
A key priority is to clarify whether steep temporal discounting is best understood as a developmentally emerging vulnerability marker, rather than merely a concomitant of unhealthy behavior. The endophenotype framework is especially useful here because it links intertemporal choice to heritable, relatively stable mechanisms that may mediate risk for addictive and related disorders. Reviews integrating behavioral genetics and behavioral economics argue that delay discounting already satisfies several endophenotypic criteria, including association with addiction liability, temporal stability, heritability, and elevation in unaffected relatives, although the evidence base remains modest and methodologically heterogeneous ref [58].

Developmental work further suggests that early self-control capacities and later discounting-related phenotypes should be situated within a life-course model. Childhood self-control predicts adult physical health, substance dependence, financial functioning, and criminal offending in a graded fashion, even after accounting for IQ and social class, implying that early regulatory traits may be upstream determinants of later unhealthy behavior ref [59]. This developmental perspective is consistent with classic delay-of-gratification findings showing long-range associations between preschool self-control and later competence, and with twin evidence that discounting is moderately heritable in adolescence ref [9], ref [10].

Genetic studies remain preliminary but point toward dopaminergic pathways and gene–environment interplay. Candidate-gene work has linked discounting to DRD2 and DRD4 variation, with evidence that combined DRD2/DRD4 profiles are associated with more impulsive intertemporal choice ref [8]. More broadly, DRD4-related susceptibility appears to moderate how early environments shape self-regulation: children carrying the 7-repeat allele show stronger associations between child-care exposure and attention/self-regulation outcomes ref [5]. Future research should therefore move beyond single-locus associations toward longitudinal, genetically informed designs that test developmental mediation, family-history aggregation, and environmentally contingent pathways from early self-regulation to later health-risk behavior ref [58], ref [5], ref [8].

subsections.section_title: Future Research Directions and Translational Implications
subsections.subsection_title: Mechanisms and Intervention Targets in Neurobehavioral Decision Systems
subsections.content:
A central mechanistic question is whether steep temporal discounting reflects a unitary preference parameter or an emergent consequence of interacting neurobehavioral systems. The competing neurobehavioral decision systems framework proposes that unhealthy choices arise when valuation signals favoring immediate reward outcompete executive control processes that support delayed outcomes ref [22]. Early neuroimaging evidence was consistent with this account, showing relatively greater engagement of limbic and paralimbic regions when choices included immediate rewards, alongside broader lateral prefrontal and parietal recruitment during intertemporal choice more generally ref [61]. Reinforcement-learning perspectives sharpen this view by suggesting that discounting may index how value is propagated over time and how model-based prospective evaluation competes with more myopic, cue-driven policies.

This systems perspective naturally points to intervention targets. Episodic future thinking is especially promising because simulating concrete future events recruits a core network linking hippocampal, medial prefrontal, and parietal regions that supports prospective construction and may increase the subjective value of delayed outcomes ref [62]. Consistent with this idea, cueing personally relevant future events has been shown to reduce discounting and enhance prefrontal-mediotemporal interactions, suggesting a tractable route for shifting choice toward longer-term health benefits ref [62]. Such findings motivate computational work on how prospective simulation changes state representation, credit assignment, and the precision of future reward estimates.

Causal neuromodulation studies further indicate that prefrontal circuitry is not merely correlationally associated with discounting. Noninvasive stimulation of dorsolateral prefrontal cortex can alter intertemporal choice, with effects depending on laterality and stimulation protocol ref [6]. More broadly, reviews of training, framing, and brain-stimulation manipulations suggest that discounting is modifiable rather than fixed, even if trait-like stability remains substantial ref [22]. The next translational step is to test mechanism-informed combinations—for example, episodic future thinking plus executive training or stimulation—and to determine whether experimentally shifting discounting produces durable improvements in smoking, diet, medication adherence, and other real-world health behaviors ref [22], ref [6].

subsections.section_title: Future Research Directions and Translational Implications
subsections.subsection_title: From Impulsivity to Compulsion Across Psychiatric and Addictive Disorders
subsections.content:
A key translational question is whether steep temporal discounting indexes a general liability for unhealthy choice, or a more specific vulnerability to the transition from impulsive action to compulsive disorder. Work across addiction science suggests that impulsivity is best treated as multidimensional rather than unitary, with delay discounting, response inhibition, and attentional control making partially dissociable contributions to substance use and relapse risk ref [24]. This distinction matters because temporal discounting may be especially relevant early in the course of use, whereas compulsive persistence despite harm may depend on additional learning and control failures.

Preclinical evidence strongly supports this staged view. In rats, high impulsivity predicts the later emergence of addiction-like cocaine seeking and punishment-resistant intake, whereas novelty reactivity predicts acquisition of self-administration but not the shift to compulsive use ref [63]. Related theoretical and empirical accounts propose that addiction progression involves a transfer from goal-directed, prefrontal control toward dorsal-striatal habit systems and diminished top-down inhibitory regulation, thereby linking impulsive choice to compulsive repetition through reinforcement-learning mechanisms of overtrained stimulus-response control and reduced sensitivity to future outcomes ref [24].

Future research should therefore move beyond cross-sectional associations between discount rates and diagnosis, and instead test longitudinal computational models spanning substance use, obsessive-compulsive spectrum conditions, binge eating, and other psychiatric disorders in which impulsive and compulsive phenotypes co-occur ref [24]. Particularly important are tasks that jointly quantify discounting, action inhibition, habit learning, punishment sensitivity, and model-based versus model-free control, so that temporal discounting can be located within a broader transdiagnostic pathway from vulnerability to entrenched compulsion ref [63], ref [24].

subsections.section_title: Future Research Directions and Translational Implications
subsections.subsection_title: Habits, Precommitment, and Behavior Change
subsections.content:
Future work should move beyond treating unhealthy behavior as a sequence of isolated intertemporal choices and instead model how repeated choice in stable contexts crystallizes into habits. Real-world evidence indicates that automaticity typically grows nonlinearly with repetition and consistent cueing, often over weeks to months, with substantial individual heterogeneity and only limited disruption from single lapses ref [64]. In health domains, habit is best understood as cue-contingent automaticity rather than mere response frequency, which helps explain why smoking, snacking, or sedentary routines can persist even when stated goals change ref [65]. This distinction is especially relevant for temporal discounting accounts: steep discounters may initiate unhealthy choices, but repeated enactment can gradually reduce the need for active valuation altogether.

A key translational implication is that interventions should target the transition from deliberative to habitual control. Human neuroimaging and outcome-devaluation work implicate posterior dorsolateral striatum/putamen in overtrained, outcome-insensitive responding, consistent with a shift toward stimulus-response control ref [66]. Related frameworks distinguishing goals from habits suggest that future computational models should explicitly capture arbitration between model-based, goal-directed control and model-free or habitual policies in naturalistic health behavior ref [67], ref [5]. This would clarify when discounting parameters predict behavior directly and when their influence is mediated or overridden by learned routines.

Precommitment offers a complementary route for behavior change because it can alter choice architecture before temptation or cue-triggered responding emerges. Experimental evidence on procrastination shows that people voluntarily impose costly deadlines, that such self-imposed constraints can improve performance relative to no structure, but that they are often suboptimal compared with well-designed external deadlines ref [6]. For health behavior, this suggests testing commitment devices that bind future choice sets—such as purchase restrictions, advance meal planning, smoking bans, or app-based lockouts—while simultaneously engineering stable cues for healthy repetition and disrupting cue exposure for unhealthy routines ref [65], ref [7], ref [8]. An important next step is to identify when precommitment scaffolds habit acquisition versus when it merely compensates for persistent self-control failure.

subsections.section_title: Future Research Directions and Translational Implications
subsections.subsection_title: Real-World Outcomes, Measurement, and Public Health Translation
subsections.content:
A central translational question is whether temporal discounting predicts consequential outcomes outside the laboratory. Longitudinal evidence suggests that early delay capacity can forecast later health risk: failure to delay gratification at age 4 is associated with greater overweight risk at age 11, even after accounting for socioeconomic factors, although maternal weight status attenuates the association, underscoring the importance of familial and environmental pathways as well as individual choice tendencies ref [41]. In adults, higher discount rates are associated with lower uptake of health maintenance behaviors, including cancer screening, dental visits, cholesterol testing, flu vaccination, exercise, and nonsmoking status, suggesting that steep discounting may act as a broad barrier to preventive investment in health capital ref [68].

At the same time, public health translation requires caution because observed associations depend in part on how discounting is measured. Measurement studies indicate that smokers discount delayed rewards more steeply than non-smokers across task variants, but also show that item order, delay horizon, and reward magnitude systematically alter estimated discounting parameters, limiting comparability across studies and highlighting the need for harmonized protocols and reporting standards ref [6]. Relatedly, evidence from influenza vaccination suggests that time preference effects on preventive behavior are detectable but modest, and often smaller than beliefs about vaccine effectiveness, anticipated side effects, and prior behavior ref [7]. Together, these findings argue for multimethod assessment, preregistered measurement choices, and greater use of ecologically valid outcomes rather than sole reliance on single-task discounting metrics.

For translation, the implication is not that discounting should replace established health behavior constructs, but that it can help identify who is least responsive to interventions framed around distant benefits. Interventions may therefore be more effective when they reduce immediate costs, increase proximal rewards, or restructure choices so that long-run benefits are made psychologically nearer. At a population level, this supports policy designs such as default enrollment, timely reminders, commitment supports, and incentive structures that compensate for present bias while preserving autonomy ref [68], ref [7].
